rationale: Start with a broad scouting gradient to maximize the chance of observing all 10 compounds while retaining weakly retained components. A midpoint temperature leaves room to explore temperature-dependent selectivity after locating the critical peak pairs.

Halve the gradient duration to reduce the last peak's retention time while testing how much of the current resolution margin can be traded for speed. Keep temperature and endpoints fixed to isolate the effect of gradient steepness.

Test lower-temperature selectivity at the fast gradient to separate the crowded middle peaks without sacrificing the zero time penalty. This isolates temperature effects and may recover full resolution more efficiently than lengthening the gradient.

Test the upper temperature limit because cooling worsened several critical separations. Heating may spread the middle cluster through selectivity changes while further shortening the last peak's retention time.

Test an intermediate temperature to balance the middle-cluster separation against the new near-coelution seen at 60 C. Keeping the gradient unchanged will clarify whether temperature alone can deliver full resolution with no time penalty.

Probe the temperature between the two warm runs, where the remaining crowded pair may reach baseline resolution before the earlier pair becomes too close. The last peak should remain comfortably within the zero-time-penalty region.

Test a steeper gradient at 50 C to shift selectivity in the remaining critical pair while retaining the earlier pair's resolution margin. The temperature results suggest an elution-order crossover, so shortening the gradient may improve separation rather than simply compress all peaks.

Lengthen the gradient slightly at the best temperature to improve the earlier critical pair's resolution. The later critical pair is already just above 1.5, and the projected last-peak time remains below 8 minutes, offering a chance of full resolution without a time penalty.

The maximum CRF is already achieved; test a slightly shallower gradient to assess a nearby alternative. Reducing the endpoint to 0.90 may improve the earlier critical separation while keeping the last peak near the zero-time-penalty window.

Test a modestly higher starting organic fraction to explore a faster alternative to the maximum-scoring method. This changes early retention and gradient selectivity, potentially increasing the narrow resolution margin while retaining a zero time penalty.

Slightly flatten the gradient from injection 10 to raise the earlier critical pair from R = 1.29 toward 1.5 while preserving the later pair's margin. The last peak should remain below 8 minutes, potentially yielding another maximum-scoring method.

Reduce the gradient slope one more step to lift the R = 1.47 pair above 1.5 while retaining the later pair's resolution margin. The predicted last-peak time is close to 8 minutes, so this tests a potentially maximum-scoring alternative with more balanced critical separations.

Test a gradient slope between injections 11 and 12 to balance resolution margin against the 8-minute time-penalty boundary. This may retain the maximum CRF while eluting the last peak slightly earlier than injection 12.

Explore a higher starting organic fraction with a shallower gradient to seek larger margins for both critical pairs. Injection 13 shows that the zero-time-penalty region extends beyond 8 minutes, leaving room to test this alternative while preserving the established maximum-scoring methods.

Lengthen injection 14's gradient to improve the R = 1.25 pair while exploiting the later pair's larger resolution margin. This tests whether a more balanced, fully resolved alternative remains within the zero-time-penalty region; the maximum CRF has already been secured.

Test a slightly shallower version of injection 12 to increase the earlier critical pair's resolution while checking that the later pair remains above 1.5. Its projected last-peak time is within the demonstrated zero-penalty range, so it may provide another maximum-scoring alternative.

With the maximum CRF already secured, explore a substantially faster alternative at 60 C. A steeper gradient may move the near-coeluting pair seen in injection 4 farther past its elution-order crossover, although compression of other pairs is a risk.

Test whether higher starting organic content moves the early critical pair farther past its crossover, while a longer gradient than injection 17 restores separation in the adjacent pair. This explores a faster alternative; the established CRF of 1.000 cannot be exceeded.

Increase starting organic content to test whether the remaining critical pair separates farther beyond its crossover while preserving the fast elution achieved in injection 18. This also checks whether compression of the earliest peaks limits this faster alternative.

Explore a cooler, moderately longer gradient as an alternative selectivity window, rather than further compressing the early peaks at high starting organic content. This may resolve the middle cluster on the opposite side of its temperature-dependent crossover; the maximum score is already secured.

Test a shallower gradient at 60 C to separate the earlier critical pair on the other side of its gradient-dependent crossover. This may deliver larger resolution margins than the 55 C methods while keeping the last peak near the demonstrated zero-time-penalty range.

Slightly flatten injection 15's gradient to improve its R = 1.57 limiting pair while retaining the other critical pair's margin. The projected last-peak time remains below 10 minutes, offering a potentially better-balanced alternative at the already-achieved maximum CRF.

Test a gradient slope between injections 15 and 22 to balance the two critical resolutions near 1.7 while slightly shortening retention relative to injection 22. This seeks a larger minimum-resolution margin among methods matching the maximum CRF already achieved.

Test whether a higher starting organic fraction combined with a shallower gradient can further improve the minimum-resolution margin of the maximum-scoring methods. Monitor both the earliest pair, which compressed at higher organic content, and the two middle critical pairs.

Use nearly the same gradient slope as injection 23, which achieved CRF 1.000 with both critical resolutions near 1.70, but shorten the programmed gradient by lowering its endpoint. All peaks are expected to elute before that endpoint reaches the outlet, preserving separation while slightly reducing retention times.
